scenes.text: Last video ended with saving instead of borrowing: two hundred dollars into an account at the end of every month, towards a first apartment, and the balance climbs. One grows and one shrinks, but they're the same kind of thing. What do these two have in common?

An annuity is a run of equal payments made at regular times, with interest compounding on the balance every period. Compounding means the interest is added to the balance, so next period it earns interest too. There are two kinds. In the first, you make equal contributions into an investment account, and interest is added at the end of each period. In the second, you invest one single sum, then make equal withdrawals from it. Same size, same gap, the same rate each period. That's the pattern to look for.

Let's test the idea. Two thousand dollars invested once and left to grow. Is that an annuity? Make a guess. It isn't. It earns compound interest, but there are no regular payments, so it's just compound interest, like the growth models in the sequences videos. Deposits of fifty, then eighty, then a hundred and ten dollars a month aren't equal, so that's not an annuity either. And putting money in whenever you have spare cash isn't regular. But two hundred dollars at the end of every quarter, with interest each quarter, is.

The next balance is one plus r, times this balance, minus M. That's exactly the loan rule. A loan has the same cash flows, seen from the lender's side. One sum goes out, and equal amounts come back.

Why does the fund run down? Each month the withdrawal is bigger than the interest, so the balance drops, and next month there's less to earn interest on. So it falls slowly at first, then faster, and runs out at the hundred and twentieth withdrawal, which is ten years. That last one is a little smaller, because the withdrawal is rounded up to the cent. If you only took out four hundred dollars, exactly the interest, the balance would stay at a hundred thousand forever. The withdrawal was set, the same way a loan repayment is set, so that the fund lasts ten years.

One more condition. In this course, interest compounds as often as the payments are made, so the rate and the count match the payments. Five hundred dollars a month for two years, at six per cent a year compounded monthly, has r equal to zero point zero zero five per month, and n equal to twenty-four months, not two. For quarterly payments, divide the annual rate by four. For fortnightly, divide by twenty-six. In this course, every payment comes at the end of its period.

Here's a way to spot one. Same size, same gap, interest every gap. In goes a contribution, or out goes a withdrawal, but always the same amount, at the same interval, with interest compounding in between.
